results.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, s=min{m,n}, and t=max{m,n}. Then D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}).
results.proof_sketch:
Assume 2≤m≤n. First run FillColumns on A transposed, using the transposed target coordinates. Its analysis remains valid for every p×q matrix without requiring p≤q: each column rotates at most p−1 times; if f columns are underfull, then every q rotations of the buffer row decrease the wrong-body potential by at least f/2. During the phase q/2^i≤f<q/2^{i−1}, the potential is at most (p−1)q/2^{i−1}, so fewer than 4p disjoint q-rotation blocks occur. Thus filling costs O(pq log q). With p=n,q=m, followed by FloatMinimums, O(N log m) pushes put exactly the correct token set in every original row.

It remains to permute within rows. An even permutation of one row is effected in O(N) pushes: Lemmas 8 and 10 factor it into two involutions having equally many transpositions, and opposite choices of the shift direction cancel all auxiliary-column side effects. If n is even, an odd row permutation is one unit row rotation followed by an even permutation. If n is odd and m is even, the odd case of Lemma 11 gives the same O(N) positional operation.

If m,n are both odd, the number of odd required row permutations is even. For each such row i choose the same adjacent transposition P_i and first apply the even permutation π_iP_i. Pair the residual P_i's. For adjacent rows, P_iP_{i+1} is a product of two L-shaped 3-cycles: with rectangle corners a,b,c,d in row-major order, (a b c)(a d c)=(a b)(c d). Each L-cycle is a four-push row-column commutator. Chaining adjacent-row gadgets implements P_rP_s in O(m) pushes because intermediate P_i's cancel. All parity repairs cost O(m²)≤O(N). Sorting all m rows therefore costs O(mN), giving O(Nm). Taking the better of this and the proved O(N log n) algorithm, and using symmetry, proves the claim.

results.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
results.proof_sketch: The preceding upper bound becomes O(mn) when s is fixed. For the lower bound, translate the sorted board simultaneously by floor(n/2) columns and floor(m/2) rows. The exact-distance calculation below gives m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2)=Ω(mn). Thus the logarithmic gap is completely closed for every fixed-width family.

results.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
results.proof_sketch:
Let H(A) be the sum, over all tokens, of cyclic horizontal distance from the token's current column to its target column; define V analogously. A row push moves n tokens one horizontal edge, so it changes H by at most n, while column pushes leave H unchanged. Hence at least ceil(H/n) row pushes are necessary. Similarly at least ceil(V/m) column pushes are necessary, and these bounds add.

For a global translation, H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b), giving the stated lower bound. It is attained by rotating every row d_n(a) times in the shortest reverse direction and every column d_m(b) times likewise. In particular, the half-translation has exact distance m floor(n/2)+n floor(m/2)=mn−[m(n mod 2)+n(m mod 2)]/2.

results.claim: A sharper general counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
results.proof_sketch: There are Q sortable configurations by the parity characterization. Any shortest word has no adjacent generator-inverse pair. Using the nominal d directed generators, the number of reduced words of length at most L is at most 1+d·((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2). If every sortable configuration were within L pushes, this quantity would be at least Q; rearranging gives the formula. Stirling's estimate yields D≥[N log N−N+O(log N)]/log(2(m+n)−1). In particular, for bounded aspect ratio this is (2−o(1))N.

results.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
results.proof_sketch: Exact breadth-first search with the seven distinct unit generators visited all 6!=720 configurations, with level sizes 1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3. Thus the diameter is 7. The configuration with rows (3,2,1) and (6,5,4) is at level 7; a shortest identity-to-configuration word is R1-left, C1, R1-left, C1, C3, R1-right, C1. The exact translation formula gives maximum translation distance 2 floor(3/2)+3 floor(2/2)=5.

final_writeup:
Writing N=mn, s=min{m,n}, and t=max{m,n}, the strongest general progress is the aspect-ratio-sensitive upper bound

D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}).

The new part is O(Ns). Transposing the filling stage puts every token into its target row in O(N log s) pushes; the filling potential proof remains valid even when the transposed matrix has more rows than columns. Once row memberships are correct, the proved involution gadget realizes each required row permutation in O(N) pushes. The parity cases can all be repaired within the same bound, including odd-by-odd boards via paired adjacent transpositions implemented by constant-length local commutators. Processing s rows costs O(Ns). Combining this with the paper's O(N log t) construction gives the displayed bound.

Consequently, D(m,n)=Θ(mn) whenever the smaller dimension is fixed. This closes the gap for all fixed-width families, but not for balanced or moderately growing dimensions: the remaining general bounds are Ω(N) and O(N·min{s,log t}), which still leave a logarithmic factor when s≥log t.

Two lower-bound tools were established. First, total cyclic horizontal and vertical token displacement gives an instance-specific certificate. It exactly determines the distance of every global torus translation and supplies explicit sortable instances requiring mn−O(m+n) pushes. Second, reduced-word counting gives the explicit factorial lower bound recorded above, asymptotic to 2N for bounded-aspect-ratio boards.

Finally, exhaustive analysis of the 2×3 Cayley graph shows that translations do not capture the true diameter: their maximum distance is 5, while the diameter is 7. Thus any attempt to prove a matching general lower bound solely through global displacement must use configurations more intricate than uniform translations.
